items.title: McCarthy was censured by his own Senate in 1954
items.claim: How did Joseph McCarthy's anti-communist campaign end?

options.text: After televised Army-McCarthy hearings exposed his methods, the Senate voted 67-22 to censure him on 2 December 1954; he died of liver failure in 1957 aged 48
He resigned and joined the Republican Party leadership

items.reveal:
McCarthy had risen on a 1950 Wheeling speech claiming 205 communists in the State Department. The Army-McCarthy hearings (April-June 1954) were televised; Army counsel Joseph Welch's 'Have you no sense of decency, sir?' on 9 June became the iconic moment.

Edward R. Murrow's CBS broadcast 'See It Now' on 9 March 1954 had already turned mainstream opinion. The Senate censure vote followed in December.

HUAC (House Un-American Activities Committee), the Hollywood blacklist, loyalty oaths and the Smith Act prosecutions continued separately and outlasted McCarthy.
items.why: McCarthyism as a phenomenon was bigger than McCarthy. His fall did not end the Red Scare — but it ended one specific style of grandstanding accusation, and television was central to both his rise and fall.

items.title: The Hundred Years War lasted 116 years
items.claim: When did the Hundred Years War begin and end?

options.text: 1337 (Edward III claims the French throne) to 1453 (Battle of Castillon) — 116 years, with long truces in between

items.reveal_title: A name invented in the 19th century
items.reveal:
The phrase 'Hundred Years War' was coined by French historians in the 1860s. Contemporaries did not see it as a single conflict but as a series of campaigns separated by long peaces (e.g. the Treaty of Brétigny, 1360).

Major English victories: Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356), Agincourt (1415). Major French recoveries: Du Guesclin's reconquests under Charles V, and Joan of Arc's relief of Orléans (1429). It ended with the French victory at Castillon in 1453 — three months before Constantinople fell.
items.why: Periodisation is a historical choice, not a fact. A '100 years' war that was actually 116, mostly truce, and named four centuries later is a useful reminder.

items.title: Constantine legalised Christianity in 313 CE but converted slowly
items.claim: When did the Roman Empire become Christian?

options.text: Constantine made Christianity the state religion in 312

The Edict of Milan (313) granted religious toleration; Constantine increasingly favoured Christianity but was baptised only on his deathbed in 337; Theodosius I made Christianity the state religion by the Edict of Thessalonica in 380
The empire remained pagan until 600 CE

items.reveal:
Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge (28 October 312) over Maxentius came after a reported vision of the Chi-Rho symbol with 'in hoc signo vinces' (in this sign you will conquer). The Edict of Milan, agreed with Licinius in 313, granted religious toleration to all.

Constantine convened the Council of Nicaea (325) and built churches across the empire. He moved the capital to Constantinople (founded 330). He was baptised on his deathbed in 337 by an Arian bishop, Eusebius of Nicomedia.

The Edict of Thessalonica (380) under Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the state religion. Pagan worship was progressively restricted; the Olympic Games were banned in 393.
items.why: Religious change at imperial scale is a process, not a moment. The 67 years between Milan and Thessalonica saw a tolerant empire become a Christian one — a transformation studied by every subsequent religious-political shift.
